lines: Before a single table exists, a schema already passed through three separate decisions.
This refresher is about telling those three apart.
A customer. An address. One can have more than one of the other.
Notice what is missing here on purpose: no numbers, no columns, nothing about a database at all.
That absence is the whole point of this level.
That phrase already says more than one address is possible.
So has the hard part already been decided, or is this level stopping short on purpose?
answer: It stops on purpose. Naming a relationship is not the same as fixing its shape.
Cardinality and storage both wait for the next level, deliberately.

lines: Now the same fact gets a shape: exactly one customer, exactly many addresses, drawn with a crow's foot.
Still no engine has been chosen. Any database product could implement this structure.
Here is the fact a third time, and now it finally has to run somewhere.
A real foreign key, a real column type, a real index underneath it.
Watch the pattern across all three: each level fixes exactly what the one before it refused to.
Fix a column type while a stakeholder is still agreeing on what a customer even is, and you have closed a door nobody meant to close yet.
In a real project built for one engine, the middle step often just disappears.
Keeping it on paper only pays off once more than one engine, or more than one logical shape, is actually in play.
Three levels, three separate jobs: what exists, how it is shaped, how it runs.
Carry that distinction forward, because the next refresher pulls the physical level in two directions at once.
